title: Profiteering Does Not Mix With Human Service
author: Peter Greene
summary: Greene uses a ProPublica story on a Washington company that took $38 million in public money for special education, and was accused by parents and former staff of cutting corners, to argue that profit and human services do not mix. He reads the case as school choice in action: funding follows the child, who becomes a courier of cash to the operators. In a market-based system the owners' interests will always conflict with children's, because profit comes from spending less on the customer. Families cannot opt out of education or medical care, which gives such businesses a captive customer base. He closes by contrasting those who see only economic motives with those who insist on keeping eyes on people's humanity and needs. This is school-policy commentary, filed with his other pieces in Practice & Culture.
points: The ProPublica case shows publicly funded special education becoming a profit venture that cuts services to the legal minimum.
Voucher-style funding turns each child into a cash carrier for operators.
Under a marketplace model the owners' interest in profit and the children's interests will conflict.
Education and health care cannot be opted out of, giving providers a built-in customer base.
Meeting only legal minimums is a warning sign when the law demands very little.
quotes: In a school choice system that is wedded to the marketplace, the interests of the owners of the education-flavored businesses will always conflict with the interests of the children. Always. And the main means of maximizing profit will always be to find ways to spend less and less serving the "customers.
Corner cutting is the least of the terrible outcomes. We have only to look at the privatized health care industry to see the worst cases in action, like this story about a hospital in Pennsylvania.
As I've said repeatedly, the goal of making a profit is not inherently evil. But it does not mix well with human services.

I can't opt out of an education for my child, especially if my child requires special accommodations to get it. That gives these sorts of operations a built in customer base, but if the service is provided by someone in search of profit, they have no incentive to provide anything but the least they can get away with and still make money.

But for folks who believe in bigger things, the problem is obvious. If you're going to take care of people, you've got to have your eyes on their humanity and needs, and not the cash strapped to their backs.
